title: POC scoping - Ember Digital - Integration planning
summary: Initial POC scoping focused on integration approach. Ember wants OpenAI-compatible endpoints + SDKs, function/tool calling for data lookups, and strict structured JSON outputs. Success criteria: p95 latency <200ms for chat flows, end-to-end throughput for 50 RPS burst, and acceptable cost per 1M tokens. Timeline: 6-week POC with benchmarks in week 2 and week 5. Action items to share architecture diagram, pricing, and a small sample repo.
next_steps: Redwood to share security & architecture doc and sample SDK repo (Maya) by 2027-03-20
Ember to provide representative prompt set + traffic shape by 2027-03-22
Schedule benchmark run week of 2027-03-29 (Ravi + Marcus)
Follow-up demo of OpenAI-compatible endpoints and function calling 2027-03-25 at 10:00 PT
action_items: Maya Chen: send security & architecture doc, sample SDK repo (due 2027-03-20)
Marcus Reid: upload representative prompt set and traffic histogram to shared folder (due 2027-03-22)
Ravi Patel: prepare benchmark harness and test plan (due 2027-03-26)
Sofia Alvarez: confirm VPC peering requirements and IP allowlist (due 2027-03-24)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Lena (Ember CTO), Marcus (Ember ML Eng), Sofia (Ember Platform Eng)

Summary/Topics (auto): integration planning, success criteria, sizing, benchmarks, timeline, SDKs, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function calling, structured output

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh I'm Maya Chen from Redwood, with me is Ravi Patel, our solutions engineer. how's everybody doing?
[00:08] Lena: good, thanks, uh excited to dig in. we wanted to be explicit about integration approach — Ember's aim is to keep dev velocity high so OpenAI-compatible APIs and SDKs are preferred.
[00:20] Marcus: yeah, and we'll need tool calling for internal lookups — think inventory and user-data service calls — and strict JSON outputs so downstream parsers don't break.
[00:30] Ravi: cool, that maps well to Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoints and function/tool-calling support. quick Q: do you expect streaming responses or full-response latencies?
[00:40] Sofia: for chat features we want streaming in product but fallbacks to non-streaming for batch jobs. p95 latency goal for interactive flows is around 150-200 ms, if possible.
[00:52] Maya: that's good context. for the POC, typical success criteria we recommend capturing: latency SLA (p95), quality parity against your current baseline, throughput/burst capacity, and unit cost per 1M tokens. does that align?
[01:06] Lena: yes. we also require SOC2-level audit logs, SSO via SAML, RBAC on keys, and KMS integrations — we'll need to validate those in the security doc.
[01:18] Maya: understood. we'll include SOC2 evidence and KMS/SSO integration notes.
[01:23] Marcus: on workload sizing — current traffic for the chat product is around 30 RPS average, with spikes to ~60 RPS. typical prompts average 250 tokens in, ~120 tokens out. also a smaller batch job that runs 5k requests nightly for indexing.
[01:38] Ravi: ok so for POC we'd plan to validate at 50 RPS sustained with 100 RPS short bursts. we'll run two bench types: latency-focused (single user interactive, KV/prefix cache warm vs cold) and throughput-focused (batched inference, quantized variants).
[01:52] Lena: what's the recommended hardware for dedicated testing versus hosted? we prefer hosted initially but may move to dedicated or private if data residency or performance issues arise.
[02:02] Ravi: for hosted we'll provision nodes in the same cloud region — typically gpus with high single-stream perf. for Dedicated we'd recommend reserved A100-ish or H100 pools depending on model. for POC hosted should be fine to validate integration and latency envelopes.
[02:16] Marcus: what about caching — we rely on KV cache for chat context; any gotchas? I heard Redwood has smart prefix caching but want to confirm warm cache expectations.
[02:26] Ravi: yep, Redwood uses prefix/KV caching and automatic hot-keying. warm-cache p95 can be significantly lower — we'll include a cache-warm vs cold run. note: transcription/notes — sometimes product names come out as 'kay vee cache' in sample docs, heh.
[02:40] Sofia: about function calling — we need deterministic JSON schemas returned from the model when calling tools, because our orchestrator expects exact fields. can Redwood force structured outputs?
[02:50] Maya: yes, we support structured output enforcement — you can provide a JSON schema and we add wrapper constraints and evals to ensure model returns match. plus we have a post-parse validity check in the runtime that flags mismatches.
[03:03] Marcus: great. also we have an internal tool that the model can call for enrichment; it requires OAuth-based service account calls. can Redwood's function calling reach out to our services securely?
[03:12] Ravi: function calling is proxied through the customer's environment for Private deployments. For hosted we can do a secure webhook pattern with signed requests and IP allowlists; for Dedicated/Private we can do VPC peering or service account flows.
[03:25] Lena: that sounds workable. timeline — Ember is targeting a demo for execs in 6 weeks. can we fit a 4-6 week POC into that window?
[03:34] Maya: yes. typical POC cadence we suggest: week 0 onboarding + security review, week 1 integration + sample SDK test, week 2 initial benchmark run (latency), week 3 iterate on prompts and models, week 4 throughput benchmark, week 5 end-to-end QA & regression checks, week 6 exec demo.
[03:50] Sofia: if we start next week it should fit. who will own the benchmark harness?
[03:55] Ravi: Redwood SE will provide harness and scripts; Marcus will run them in your environment and share results or we can run from Redwood infra against your test endpoints depending on desired isolation.
[04:06] Marcus: we'd prefer to run them against our staging endpoints. we'll instrument request traces and token counts and share results.
[04:12] Maya: perfect. on integration specifics — we expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so minimal code changes for you. we also have language-specific SDKs (python, node, go) with helpers for function/tool calling and structured-output enforcement.
[04:26] Marcus: can you share a short sample? even a skeleton is fine.
[04:29] Ravi: yes — we'll send a small repo with examples: chat stream with function call, non-stream batch call, and structured json schema enforcement.
[04:38] Lena: about rate limits and quotas — Ember has internal limits around RPS per key; can Redwood do per-route rate limits and token quotas?
[04:47] Maya: yes, per-route rate limits, per-key quotas, and token budgeting are supported in the console. we can map to your RBAC roles too.
[04:55] Sofia: what about observability — we need token-level cost breakdown and tracing to correlate user sessions to model calls.
[05:02] Ravi: Redwood Console provides token/cost breakdown by route/model, per-request tracing IDs, and hooks for your ingest to correlate session IDs. we'll include sample dashboards.
[05:12] Marcus: will the POC test multiple model variants/quantization profiles? we want to see quality vs cost tradeoffs.
[05:19] Maya: yes — POC will include a couple model variants (e.g., base open model and a quantized variant) and we'll run A/B compare on quality metrics you provide.
[05:27] Lena: what are acceptable benchmarks for quality? we can provide a labeled eval set for intent/slot accuracy, and a small human eval for generative quality.
[05:36] Maya: that's perfect — labeled evals plus a small human review. that'll let us produce regression alerts in Redwood Optimize.
[05:44] Sofia: privacy/regulatory note — some data must remain in-region, is Redwood able to pin region and ensure data residency?
[05:51] Ravi: yes, for Hosted we can pin region, and for Private we support on-prem or VPC deployments. we'll document data flow and retention.
[05:59] Marcus: about costs — can we get an estimate for the POC run (benchmark compute + token costs)? we need to budget for infra and plan for the exec deck.
[06:06] Maya: we'll produce a POC estimate: cost breakdown by benchmark runs (GPU-hours) and token consumption. I'll include a rough estimate in the follow-up doc.
[06:13] Lena: ok good. any blockers on our side?
[06:16] Sofia: we need to confirm network allowlist and SAML metadata, and get the prompt sets. we'll do that this week.
[06:23] Marcus: one small ask — can Redwood's SDK emit typed response objects in our codegen? our platform uses generated types to parse responses.
[06:30] Ravi: absolutely — our SDKs have a codegen helper that can produce typed wrappers from the JSON schema you provide; we'll show an example in the repo.
[06:39] Maya: quick recap of next steps before we run out: we'll send security & architecture doc + sample SDK repo by 2027-03-20; you (Ember) will upload prompt set and traffic histogram by 2027-03-22; SE will prepare benchmark harness by 2027-03-26; schedule the live demo and benchmark week of 2027-03-29.
[06:56] Lena: sounds good. one more thing — competitors, we're also looking at Anthropic and OpenAI, mainly to compare latency and cost.
[07:05] Maya: noted. we'll include side-by-side baseline comparisons where possible.
[07:09] Sofia: ok thanks everyone.
[07:12] Marcus: thanks.
[07:14] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and repo.

[End of meeting]

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-transcriptions of acronyms (e.g., 'kay vee cache' for KV cache); speaker labels are largely accurate but some timestamps may shift slightly. Links referenced during call: - security & architecture doc (to be attached) - sample SDK repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/pocexamples/tree/ember-sample (will attach in follow-up) - benchmark harness & scripts (to be shared by SE)
